title: Archimedes Defends Syracuse
text:
In 214 BC the Roman general Marcellus attacked Syracuse, the great Greek city of Sicily, by land and sea. He expected a quick success. Instead, Polybius and Plutarch say, he met the machines of Archimedes, the city's aged mathematician.

Catapults of different ranges threw stones and missiles, so that ships were struck at every distance as they approached. When Roman ships came close under the sea walls, cranes swung out and dropped heavy weights on them. Other machines lowered an iron grip, often called the claw, that hooked a ship's prow, lifted it out of the water and let it fall, so that it capsized or was smashed. Marcellus's floating siege tower on lashed ships was wrecked. On land, attackers were struck by missiles through small openings in the walls.

Plutarch writes that the Romans became so frightened that if they saw a rope or a beam projecting over the wall, they turned and fled, shouting that Archimedes was about to use some engine on them. Marcellus gave up assault and settled down to a blockade.

The city held out for more than two years. In 212 BC the Romans took part of it by surprise during a festival, and the rest fell soon after. In the sack, Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier, reportedly while absorbed in a geometric problem. Plutarch says Marcellus was grieved by his death.
lesson: Ingenuity can multiply the strength of a small side, but it buys time rather than certainty. Use the time it buys to solve the larger problem.
source: Polybius, Histories 8.3 to 8.7; Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14 to 19
caveat: The story that Archimedes burned Roman ships with mirrors appears only in much later writers and is probably legend.
